items.title: Valence and levels of explanation
items.student: Supplied outer-electron counts:H1,O6,N5,Na1,Cl7,Al3. Classify these explanatory records:Na transfers one electron toCl and the resulting opposite ions attract;twoH atoms share an electron pair;Al solid contains positive ion cores and delocalised electrons;separate water molecules attract through hydrogen bonding. Identify ionic,covalent,metallic and intermolecular descriptions. Explain why the source's list includes both bonds within structures and attractions between molecules. Source lists H2,O2,iodine,diamond,graphite among examples;these are elements,not compounds. Water/NaCl are compounds. Draw one labelled representation and name what it omits.
items.teacher: IonicNaCl,covalentH2,metallicAl,hydrogen attraction between water molecules. Electron transfer alone is not the ionic bond;electrostatic attraction between opposite ions is essential. Shared-pair covalent bond is distinct from intermolecular attractions. All named element/compound distinctions explicit. A schematic does not establish size,energy or physical testing.

items.title: Ionic transfer and extended structure
items.student: Draw before/after outer-electron dot/cross diagrams forNaCl andMgO usingNa1,Cl7,Mg2,O6. Use dots for nonmetal-original electrons,crosses for transferred metal electrons,brackets and charges. Inner shells may be omitted if stated. Then draw a small labelled alternating-ion lattice fragment and explain why a NaCl formula unit is an ion ratio,not a single molecule. Predict conductivity of solid versus molten NaCl from fixed versus mobile ions;no melting is performed.
items.teacher: Na loses1 electron to become Na+; Cl gains1 and has7 dots+1 cross. Mg loses2 to become Mg2+; O gains2 and has6 dots+2 crosses. Both formula ratios1:1. Lattice sketch labels alternating charges and a continuing pattern. Ions are fixed in the solid,so ordinary ionic conduction is absent; molten ions can move and carry charge. A fragment is schematic and does not imply each ion attracts only one neighbour.

items.title: Covalent dot and cross drawings
items.student: Draw dot/cross outer-electron diagrams forH2,H2O,O2,N2 andI2. Counts:H1,O6,N5,I7. Show single,double/triple shared pairs as appropriate and all lone pairs. Explain bonding within each molecule separately from attractions between molecules. ClassifyH2O as compound andH2,O2,N2,I2 as elemental molecules. State why boiling molecular water does not normally break its internalO–H bonds intoH/O atoms.
items.teacher: H2: one shared pair,no lone pairs. H2O: two O–H shared pairs,two O lone pairs. O2: two shared pairs,two lone pairs per O. N2: three shared pairs,one lone pair per N. I2: one shared pair,three lone pairs per I. Each H has a duet and the others an octet in these Lewis models. Boiling separates water molecules by overcoming intermolecular attractions,without decomposing them. Dot/cross marks origins rather than different electron species.

items.title: Dative-covalent formation and equivalent bonds
items.student: Supplied record:NH3 has threeN–H bonds and a nitrogen lone pair;H+ has no electron. Draw a dot/cross diagram forNH3 then an electron-pair donor arrowN→H+ and bracketedNH4+. Show how the donated pair forms a coordinate/dative covalent bond. Count all valence electrons and total charge. Explain why in the formed ammonium ion all fourN–H bonds are equivalent even though a formation diagram labels one pair's origin. No ammonia or acid is handled.
items.teacher: NH3 has8 outer electrons (5+3),three bond pairs and one N lone pair. NH4+ has8 (5+4−1),all four pairs bonding and total charge+1. Both electrons of the new bond originated on N; after formation all four N–H bonds are equivalent. The arrow indicates pair donation to H+,not a permanently distinct weak bond. Do not confuse Lewis formal charge with nitrogen oxidation number.

items.title: Intermolecular attractions and property claims
items.student: Supplied diagrams to draw:two water molecules,each with solidO–H covalent connections;markpartialδ−onO andδ+onH,then a dottedO···H attraction between molecules. A second record is twoI2 molecules with strong internalI–I covalent bonds and weaker dispersion attractions between molecules. Label hydrogen bonding and van der Waals/dispersion attractions separately. Explain why all molecules can have dispersion forces but not all can hydrogen-bond like water. Compare the forces overcome on boiling water versus separating iodine molecules,without claiming the internal bonds disappear. References:IUPAC hydrogen-bond recommendations https://publications.iupac.org/pac/83/8/1637/index.html;van der Waals forces https://goldbook.iupac.org/terms/view/V06597/pdf. Definitions are paraphrased for this level,not a universal strength ranking.
items.teacher: Solid connections inside molecules are covalent. Dotted water O···H represents an intermolecular hydrogen bond. I2 has dispersion attractions but no water-like hydrogen bonding. Dispersion is a van der Waals component; do not call every attraction covalent or hydrogen bonding. Boiling overcomes intermolecular cohesion while molecules remain. Avoid claiming every hydrogen bond exceeds every dispersion interaction; size,geometry and context matter.

items.title: Metallic bonding as a collective model
items.student: Supplied aluminium model:manyAl positiveioncores in an extended structure with delocalised valence electrons. Draw and label a small continuing fragment with a mobile-electron sea and attraction between cores/electrons. Explain electrical conduction,thermal transfer and malleability at this level;do not claim every atom forms an isolatedAl3+molecule. Compare moving electrons in metal with moving ions in moltenNaCl. No circuit or heating is operated.
items.teacher: Metallic cohesion involves attraction between positive cores and delocalised electrons. Mobile electrons in solid Al support electrical conduction. Electrons and the lattice contribute to thermal transfer; metals are not the only thermal conductors. Collective bonding supports layers shifting without immediate brittle separation. Molten NaCl conducts through ions,unlike the electron carriers in metal. The Al3+-core/three-electron model is simplified bookkeeping,not a population of isolated free ions.

items.title: Structure comparison from complete reference data
items.student: Supplied text table:NaCl—giantionic lattice,solid doesnot conduct,molten conducts,high melting point,soluble in water under ordinary conditions;I2—simple molecular solid,weakdispersion between molecules,poor conductor,low solubility in water;diamond—giantcovalent3D network,hard,electricalinsulator;graphite—giantcovalent layeredcarbon,conducts along layers,layers slide;Al—giantmetallic,conducts in solidstate,malleable. Classify each structure;relate one property to particle arrangement/carriers or forces. Explain why 'all covalent substances have low melting points' and 'all high melting substances are ionic' fail. Reference:OpenStax Chemistry2e https://openstax.org/books/chemistry-2e/pages/10-5-the-solid-state-of-matter (structure categories);specific records here are teaching summaries.
items.teacher: Categories follow the supplied records. Diamond and graphite refute the claim that every covalent substance has a low melting point; network diamond refutes the claim that every high-melting solid is ionic. I2 is molecular,not giant covalent. Graphite conducts through delocalised electrons within layers while its strong covalent framework remains. Solubility alone does not establish bond type; not all ionic solids dissolve.

items.title: Investigating properties with provenance
items.student: Supplied reference table; no high-temperature tests: NaCl melts at about801°C; Al about660°C; pure water melts about0°C and boils about100°C at101kPa. NaCl dissolves in water; iodine only sparingly. Pure water has low electrical conductivity compared with ionic salt solution; Al and graphite conduct. Design fair tests for solubility,electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity,and explain what the melting/boiling records show. Optional actual low-risk solubility observation,only with teacher approval: known food-grade salt in room-temperature water using approved clean equipment. Record actual amounts,conditions and outcome; those are not supplied here. No tasting,iodine handling,flames,hot objects,mains electricity or molten-substance heating. If approval/resources are unavailable,use the supplied data and mark actual investigation not performed. Pressure,purity,temperature and measurement conditions matter.
items.teacher: A solubility comparison holds solvent amount,temperature,mixing and observation time constant. Known sample identity is required; dissolving does not establish identity. Conductivity needs approved low-voltage equipment and safe contacts; thermal tests need a qualified protocol and must not involve touching hot metal. These design tasks supply no permission or apparatus. Heating to801°C or660°C is not learner work here. Water's boiling point depends on pressure; the record is not a local measurement. Count actual salt observation only if performed and avoid quantitative claims without measured amounts. Explain properties through structure,forces and mobile carriers.

items.title: Diamond and graphite:one element,different structures
items.student: Supplied structure records: diamond—each C covalently linked to4 others in a3D network,no ordinary mobile electrons,very hard. Graphite—each C linked to3 within layers,delocalised electrons in layers,weaker attractions between layers. Draw labelled fragments and compare bond type,structure,electrical behaviour and hardness/sliding. Select one for a cutting abrasive and one for a pencil marking material; justify and state a limit. Do not scratch,sample or heat diamonds or unknown powders. Reference: RSC Carbon,https://periodic-table.rsc.org/element/6/carbon.
items.teacher: Both are giant covalent carbon allotropes,not different elements or I2-like molecules. Diamond's hard network suits abrasive cutting; graphite's sliding layers suit pencil marks or lubrication,subject to grade/product conditions. Graphite's softness/conduction does not mean weak covalent bonds within layers. Label interlayer forces and delocalisation; fragments are schematic. Diamond can conduct heat well while electrically insulating; avoid equating electrical and thermal insulation.

items.title: Aluminium cookware:properties and product limits
items.student: Supplied decision facts: Al metal conducts heat,is lightweight and malleable,and has a protective oxide surface. Actual cookware may be alloyed,coated or anodised. The product's instructions,stove compatibility and condition must be checked; bond type alone does not certify every product for every food or use. Explain metallic structure links to two useful properties. Draft questions for a manufacturer without inventing medical claims. Audit this fictional message: 'Any Al pan works on every hob; bond type proves all coatings safe; clean it with anything.' Correct each claim. Reference: RSC Aluminium,https://periodic-table.rsc.org/element/13/aluminium,for general properties; no product-specific manual is supplied.
items.teacher: Mobile electrons and lattice behaviour support heat transfer; metallic bonding supports forming. Low density is useful but does not follow from bond type alone. Actual manufacturer instructions must establish product compatibility,coating care and cleaning. No all-foods/all-hobs/all-cleaners or health verdict. This is a message draft; no cooking,cleaning or delivery is inferred. Do not supply cleaning recipes or recommend abrading coatings.

items.title: Select materials from supplied constraints
items.student: Fictional jobs: A needs an electrical contact in a solid device; B needs a hard abrasive; C needs a sliding marking material; D needs a light,formable heat-transfer container with manufacturer approval. Available materials with the supplied CB7/CB9/CB10 properties: NaCl,I2,diamond,graphite,Al. Choose a supported material for each job,link structure/carriers/forces to its useful property,and state one practical uncertainty. No prices,dimensions or product certificates are given. Reflect on one way an initial choice based only on bond type changed after considering structure and conditions. No device is assembled.
items.teacher: A: Al or graphite with supported conductivity and contact/product limits. B: diamond. C: graphite. D: Al subject to product compatibility. Solid NaCl is not an ordinary conductor; I2 is a poor conductor; diamond is not an ordinary electrical contact. No exact cost or best-overall claim follows. Reflection names a change in reasoning and its evidence,not a persistent attitude or financial saving.

items.title: Build actual molecule and lattice models
items.student: Project1: plan then construct a H2O or O2 molecular model AND a NaCl alternating-ion lattice fragment using approved clean scrap card/paper and safe connectors. Include a labelled key,correct charges,molecular bond multiplicity and lattice continuation. Explain why the ionic fragment is not a NaCl molecule and why ball/stick sizes are schematic. Peer-check and revise actual products; record materials used without inventing savings. If construction cannot occur,submit a plan and mark project not performed. Optional actual digital activity requires a teacher-approved virtual bond lab or simulation with title,link and action record. The printed CB2–CB6 representations are a paper alternative and do not prove digital navigation. Label each product as simple molecular or giant ionic structure,and explain the distinguishing particle arrangement.
items.teacher: H2O model: two O–H bonds with bent connectivity,and two O lone pairs if shown. O2: double bond. NaCl: alternating signs and extended structure;1:1 ratio for complete formula units,without insisting every arbitrary boundary fragment has equal numbers. Assess actual model/key/revision evidence; a plan alone is insufficient. Ionic crystals are not made of NaCl molecules. Approve small parts,connectors and accessibility. Teacher supplies/previews any simulation; none is claimed embedded or viewed.

items.title: Prepare an honest community-care message
items.student: Project2: use CB10's facts and limits to draft an Al cookware use/care message for a fictional audience. Include one property-use benefit,two questions needing an actual manufacturer's instructions,one practical care limit,and the line 'Draft: not yet delivered.' Plan review and permission before any school-approved presentation. Record an actual audience,date and feedback only if delivery occurs. Audit: 'Our draft proves we changed community behaviour and all such pans are safe.' Explain why unperformed outreach remains unperformed and why a bond model cannot certify product health or safety.
items.teacher: Heat transfer and forming are useful links. Product questions can cover coating care,cleaning,stove compatibility and use conditions. A draft is not delivery or behaviour change. Avoid health claims or unapproved care procedures. Source community sensitisation needs actual approved action; this written task does not complete it. Record observed communication/respect only,not lasting patriotism or disposition.

items.title: Final-only bonding and selection record
items.student: HELD-OUT FINAL REFERENCE. Outer counts: Mg2,F7,N5,H1,O6. Material records: MgF2—giant ionic,solid poor conductor,molten conducts. H2O—simple molecules,covalent O–H inside,hydrogen attractions between molecules. NH4+—four equivalent N–H bonds after NH3 lone-pair donation to H+. Diamond—3D carbon network with4 neighbours,hard,electrical insulator. Graphite—carbon layers with3 neighbours,delocalised electrons and sliding layers. Al—extended metallic structure,solid conductor,malleable,lightweight. All properties are supplied,not student tests. Fictional jobs: solid electrical contact,hard abrasive,and formable heat-transfer container requiring product-manual approval. No prices or product certificates. In the water drawing,mark partial charges and one intermolecular attraction. Dot/cross key: dots for non-metal original electrons,crosses for transferred metal electrons; state omitted inner shells. For ammonium show pair origin without claiming one final bond differs. No actual project,digital or community-performance record is supplied.
items.teacher: I1: Mg transfers one electron to each of two F atoms,forming Mg2+ and two F−; each F has7 dots+1 cross,with brackets/charges. Water has two shared pairs and two O lone pairs; δ−O/δ+H and dotted O···H between molecules. Ammonium formed from NH3+H+ has four bond pairs/8 outer electrons; final bonds equivalent. I2: distinguish ionic,molecular,giant covalent and metallic structures. Molten MgF2 has mobile ions; Al and graphite have mobile electrons; diamond electrical insulation is not thermal insulation. I3: contact Al or graphite with justified limits; abrasive diamond; container Al subject to manual. I4: reflect on a material-choice constraint and a model limit. Written work does not prove model construction,outreach or digital use.
